statement: The restricting factor for scaling a relational database is that its relations and consistency guarantees need all the data to be in one place; non-relational databases typically do not give you these features, so they are not bound by it.
detail: Said between the backstory (relational databases chose consistency over ingestion rate) and the fix (drop foreign keys to partition). It is the causal link between the two, which no part item states.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if this is the restricting factor where you need all the data to be in one place and whatnot

statement: One more reason Slack persists a message before delivering it: its users do not each keep their own separate storage of the messages (unlike WhatsApp, where a copy is stored on the user's local mobile).
detail: Said as the bridge from the Slack flow to the WhatsApp example; the contrast with WhatsApp's local copy follows in the same paragraph. Reading it as a reason for Slack's synchronous persistence comes from the context ("Because also one more reason"), not from an explicit sentence.
case_study: Slack (the case study of this part).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because also one more reason, because not each user has a separate storage.
flags: check: "not each user has a separate storage" read as a reason for Slack's synchronous persistence

statement: Because persistence already happens on the user's device (one copy of every message is stored there), a WhatsApp-like app can do its backend persistence asynchronously.
detail: This is the teacher's justification for the type-2 'green line' flow (WebSocket -> edge server -> Kafka -> database later); persistence right away is not what is being guaranteed. Hypothetical: the teacher repeats that WhatsApp does not actually store messages in a backend.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So given this, where persistence is anywhere happening on a user device and I can very well do this part asynchronously.
